lesson.title: The Voltage Spike When a Coil Loses Its Source
lesson.summary: When the source driving an inductor is suddenly removed, the current cannot stop instantly and instead decays exponentially through whatever path remains, often producing a large voltage spike that is the reason inductive loads need flyback protection.
lesson.body:
An inductor's defining habit works against it, not for it, the moment its source disappears. The physical reason is the same one from RL energizing: current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, because doing so would require an infinite rate of change of magnetic flux and therefore an infinite induced voltage. So when a switch opens or a source is suddenly removed from a coil that was carrying a steady current I0, that current does not stop, it keeps flowing, now driven by the inductor's own collapsing magnetic field, seeking whatever path is available, in this case a resistor left in the loop. This is RL de-energizing, and unlike energizing, the initial condition here is a nonzero current, not zero.

With the source gone and the inductor now discharging its stored energy through R, the current follows i(t) = I0*e^(-tR/L), decaying from its starting value toward zero with the familiar time constant tau = L/R. The voltage across the resistor, and by Kirchhoff's law across the inductor as well, is v(t) = i(t)*R = I0*R*e^(-tR/L), largest at the very instant the source is removed and then decaying away along with the current.

That instant is exactly where the danger lives. At t = 0, the current has not yet had time to decay, so v jumps immediately to I0*R, a value set entirely by how much current was flowing and how large the remaining resistance is, with no regard for what the original source voltage happened to be. If the remaining resistance is large, or if the current is interrupted by an open switch instead of being routed through a deliberate resistor, this voltage spike can be dramatic, because an open switch behaves like an extremely large resistance and the inductor will develop whatever voltage it takes to keep its current flowing, even arcing across the gap of the switch itself.

Suppose a coil with L = 0.5 H has been carrying a steady I0 = 3 A and is then switched to discharge through R = 25 ohms. The time constant is tau = L/R = 0.5/25 = 0.02 seconds, or 20 milliseconds. At t = 20 ms, one time constant, the current has fallen to i = 3*e^-1 = 3*0.3679 = 1.104 A. But look at the voltage the instant the switch opens: v(0) = I0*R = 3*25 = 75 V, a full 75 volt spike arising from a circuit that might only have been running on a 12 or 24 volt supply. This is the textbook explanation for why switching off a relay coil or a motor winding produces a spark at the switch contacts, and why real designs add a flyback diode or snubber network across the coil, giving the collapsing current a controlled, lower voltage path instead of an open circuit to arc across.

Every joule the coil released has to go somewhere, and here it all ends up as heat in R. The energy stored at the start was (1/2)*L*I0^2 = 0.5*0.5 H*9 A^2 = 2.25 J, and by the time the current reaches zero, all 2.25 J has been dissipated in the resistor, the inductive twin of a capacitor dumping its stored energy into a resistor during RC discharging.
